claim: 32 subjects performed a synchronization-continuation tapping task (SCT) with auditory or visual metronomes and five tempos ranging from 550 to 950 ms.
source: Diffusion-weighted images were obtained from 32 subjects who performed the SCT with auditory or visual metronomes and five tempos ranging from 550 to 950 ms.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of subjects, task type, modalities, and tempo range used in the study.

claim: Individual differences in the density of U-fibers in the right audiomotor system were correlated with the degree of phase accuracy between the stimuli and taps across subjects.
source: Notably, individual differences in the density of U-fibers in the right audiomotor system were correlated with the degree of phase accuracy between the stimuli and taps across subjects.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated in the abstract, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The correlations between U-fiber density and phase accuracy were specific to the synchronization epoch with auditory metronomes and tempos around 1.5 Hz.
source: These correlations were specific to the synchronization epoch with auditory metronomes and tempos around 1.5 Hz.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the specificity of the correlations to particular task conditions and tempo ranges.

claim: A significant association was found between phase accuracy and the density and bundle diameter of the corpus callosum (CC).
source: In addition, a significant association was found between phase accuracy and the density and bundle diameter of the corpus callosum (CC), forming an interval-selective map where short and long intervals were behaviorally correlated with the anterior and posterior portions of the CC.
evidence: This finding is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by fixel-based analysis data presented in the results.

claim: Short and long intervals were behaviorally correlated with the anterior and posterior portions of the corpus callosum, respectively.
source: In addition, a significant association was found between phase accuracy and the density and bundle diameter of the corpus callosum (CC), forming an interval-selective map where short and long intervals were behaviorally correlated with the anterior and posterior portions of the CC.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes an interval-selective topographic map in the corpus callosum.

claim: Humans can entrain to auditory beats across a wide range of tempos.
source: Indeed, humans are extremely sensitive to auditory regularities and can entrain to auditory beats across a wide range of tempos, as well as use timed movements of different body parts (such as finger or foot taps or body swaying) to keep the beat (Mendoza and Merchant, 2014; Repp and Su, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research in the field.

claim: Humans show negative asynchronies during synchronization-continuation tasks, tapping a few milliseconds before the metronome.
source: In this type of task, humans show negative asynchronies, namely they tap a few milliseconds before the metronome, supporting the notion that entrainment depends on a predictive internal beat that is phase-locked to the stimuli (Lenc et al., 2021; Repp and Su, 2013; Zarco et al., 2009).
evidence: This behavioral phenomenon is described with supporting citations from the literature.

claim: The internal beat representation during an SCT rests in the motor system, including the basal ganglia and supplementary motor regions.
source: Neurophysiological and functional imaging studies have shown that the internal beat representation during an SCT rests in the motor system, including the basal ganglia and supplementary motor regions (Bartolo et al., 2014; Merchant et al., 2013a; Merchant and Averbeck, 2017; Rao et al., 2001; Sánchez-Moncada et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to neurophysiological and imaging studies.

claim: Neurons in the supplementary motor areas (SMAs) are tuned to the tempo duration of tapping.
source: In addition, neurons in the supplementary motor areas (SMAs) are tuned to the tempo duration of tapping (Merchant et al., 2014a; Merchant et al., 2013b), giving rise to interval-specific circuits that define a chronotopic map with short preferred intervals in the anterior portion and long preferred intervals in the posterior portion of the medial premotor areas (Protopapa et al., 2019; Merchant et al., 2024b).
evidence: This claim about neural tuning is supported by citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: Interval-specific circuits define a chronotopic map with short preferred intervals in the anterior portion and long preferred intervals in the posterior portion of the medial premotor areas.
source: In addition, neurons in the supplementary motor areas (SMAs) are tuned to the tempo duration of tapping (Merchant et al., 2014a; Merchant et al., 2013b), giving rise to interval-specific circuits that define a chronotopic map with short preferred intervals in the anterior portion and long preferred intervals in the posterior portion of the medial premotor areas (Protopapa et al., 2019; Merchant et al., 2024b).
evidence: This topographic organization is described with supporting citations.

claim: Humans demonstrate a spontaneous rhythmic tempo around 600–750 ms.
source: This spontaneous or preferred tempo is around 600–750 ms in human adults (Fischl, 2012; Fraisse, 1978, but see Parncutt, 1994), but is faster in early childhood and slower in late adulthood (McAuley et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim about spontaneous tempo is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The perception of rhythmic stimuli has a preferred tempo with an optimal sampling rate of ~1.4 Hz (ISI of 714 ms) in audition and ~0.7 Hz (ISI of 1428 ms) in vision.
source: A recent study demonstrated that the perception of rhythmic stimuli also has a preferred tempo, with an optimal sampling rate of ~1.4 Hz (ISI of 714 ms) in audition and ~0.7 Hz (ISI of 1428 ms) in vision.
evidence: This claim is based on a recent study cited in the text.

claim: Motor tapping helps to synchronize the temporal fluctuations of attention with maximal effects at ~1.7 Hz (ISI of 588 ms), but only for the auditory modality.
source: Furthermore, motor tapping helps to synchronize the temporal fluctuations of attention with maximal effects at ~1.7 Hz (ISI of 588 ms), but only for the auditory modality (Zalta et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zalta et al., 2020.

claim: There are wide individual differences in the period and phase of movement synchronization across humans.
source: Although rhythmic entrainment is prevalent across all human cultures and is a natural behavior for social interaction (Nettle, 2000; Jacoby et al., 2024), there are wide individual differences in the period (inter-tap interval) and phase (asynchronies) of movement synchronization.
evidence: This claim about individual variability is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Around 10% of the population are poor synchronizers who show low period accuracy and large asynchronies to isochronous metronomes and musical excerpts.
source: Conversely, there are poor synchronizers (around 10% of the population) that show low period accuracy and large asynchronies to isochronous metronomes and musical excerpts (Phillips-Silver et al., 2011; Sowiński and Dalla Bella, 2013; Tranchant et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim about the prevalence of poor synchronizers is supported by citations.

claim: A large-scale genome-wide association study demonstrated a highly polygenic architecture of the human capacity to synchronize to a musical beat.
source: A large-scale genome-wide association study (GWAS) recently demonstrated a highly polygenic architecture of the human capacity to synchronize to a musical beat. The GWAS phenotype for beat synchronization was related to performance in beat synchronization tasks and rhythm perception tasks (Niarchou et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a GWAS study.

claim: Genetic influences account for only a small portion of human variation in beat synchronization, while environmental influences are the primary drivers of rhythmic accuracy.
source: Nevertheless, genetic influences account for only a small portion of human variation in beat synchronization, while environmental influences are the primary drivers of rhythmic accuracy.
evidence: This claim about the relative contributions of genetic and environmental factors is stated in the introduction.

claim: Individual differences in beat perception depend on activation differences in the SMA and the posterior auditory cortex.
source: In fact, functional imaging has revealed that individual differences in beat perception depend on activation differences in the SMA and the posterior auditory cortex (Grahn and McAuley, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a functional imaging study.

claim: The putamen, SMA, and auditory cortex show greater functional connectivity during rhythm perception, with larger modulation for musicians than non-musicians.
source: In addition, the putamen, SMA, and auditory cortex show greater functional connectivity during rhythm perception, with larger modulation for musicians than non-musicians (Grahn and Rowe, 2009; Grahn and Rowe, 2013).
evidence: This claim about functional connectivity differences is supported by citations.

claim: U-fibers are short-range fibers that run tangentially to the cortical surface and connect adjacent and proximal cortical regions.
source: Long-range anatomical connectivity is supported by deep white matter (DWM) bundles, while short-range connectivity is achieved through fibers that run tangentially to the cortical surface and connect adjacent and proximal cortical regions. These fibers are collectively termed U-fibers due to their shape (Schüz and Braitenberg, 2002; Schmahmann et al., 2006, Shastin et al., 2022).
evidence: This definition of U-fibers is provided with supporting citations.

claim: Absolute asynchronies showed significant main effects for duration and modality, with significantly larger asynchronies for the visual than auditory modality across all durations.
source: The ANOVA showed significant main effects for duration (F(4,124) = 36.88, p < 0.0001) and modality (F(1,31) = 20, p < 0.0001), as well as a significant duration × modality interaction (F(4,124) = 32.3, p < 0.0001). Tukey's honest significant difference (HSD) post hoc test showed significantly larger asynchronies for the visual than auditory modality across all durations (p < 0.0001 for 550, 650, 750, and 850 ms; p = 0.006 for 950 ms; with the interaction effect mainly driven by the difference in the 950 ms across modalities).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: There was a significant correlation between absolute asynchronies at 650 and 750 ms intervals for both the auditory and visual conditions.
source: In addition, we computed the intersubject correlation matrix on the absolute asynchronies across instructed intervals and found a significant correlation between 650 and 750 ms for both the auditory and visual conditions (r = 0.67, p = 0.000026; r = 0.69, p = 0.000011, respectively) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This correlation is reported with statistical values and referenced to a figure.

claim: Lag 1 autocorrelation across trials was negative (~80% of the trials) and similar across modalities and target durations.
source: Thus, lag 1 autocorrelation across trials was negative (~80% of the trials) and similar across modalities and target durations, supporting the notion of a robust and amodal error correction mechanism during the SCT.
evidence: This finding is stated based on the analysis of autocorrelation data.

claim: During continuation, the constant error followed the bias effect, with overestimation for short durations and underestimation for long durations, especially for the auditory condition.
source: In fact, for the continuation epoch, the constant error followed the bias effect, with overestimation for short durations and underestimation for long durations, especially for the auditory condition (Jazayeri and Shadlen, 2010; Pérez and Merchant, 2018; Pérez et al., 2023).
evidence: This behavioral pattern is described with supporting citations.

claim: The indifference interval was 654 ms for the auditory condition and 420 ms for the visual condition.
source: Indeed, the indifference interval, which corresponds to the interval associated with zero constant error, was 654 ms for the auditory condition (Figure 2D, blue arrow) and 420 ms for the visual condition.
evidence: These specific values are reported from the data analysis and shown in a figure.

claim: Temporal variability showed significantly greater values in the visual metronome than in the auditory metronome during the synchronization but not the continuation epoch.
source: The HSD post hoc tests showed significantly greater temporal variability in the visual metronome than in the auditory metronome (for the intervals 650, 750, 850, and 950 ms: p < 0.0001) during the synchronization but not the continuation epoch, confirming the high period precision for auditory metronomes, especially during synchronization (Figure 2E; Gámez et al., 2018; Repp and Penel, 2004).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and referenced to a figure and citations.

claim: Negative correlations were found between auditory absolute asynchronies and values of the AFD maps in the five depths sampled.
source: This analysis showed the existence of negative correlations between the auditory absolute asynchronies and values of the AFD maps in the five depths sampled (Figure 3E–G; also see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This correlation is reported based on surface-based analysis and shown in figures.

claim: Subjects with auditory asynchronies closer to zero had significantly higher AFD and tanAFD values than subjects with less predictive performance.
source: Thus, subjects with auditory asynchronies closer to zero, and hence with larger predictive abilities, had significantly higher AFD and tanAFD values than subjects with less predictive performance.
evidence: This relationship between behavioral performance and structural measures is stated based on the analysis.

claim: Significant associations between AFD maps and behavioral parameters were observed mainly for the auditory asynchronies of the 650 and 750 ms intervals and the totalAFD and tanAFD values.
source: Notably, these significant associations were observed mainly for the auditory asynchronies of the 650 and 750 ms intervals and the totalAFD and tanAFD values (see Figure 3—videos 1–3).
evidence: This specificity of the associations is reported based on the analysis and referenced to videos.

claim: No significant correlations were found between the three AFD maps and the constant error, temporal variability, and lag 1 autocorrelation for the auditory condition.
source: No significant correlations were found between the three AFD maps and the constant error, temporal variability, and lag 1 autocorrelation for the auditory condition.
evidence: This null finding is explicitly stated in the results.

claim: No correlations were observed between the three metrics of the SWM and all the behavioral parameters for the visual condition.
source: Furthermore, no correlations were observed between the three metrics of the SWM and all the behavioral parameters for the visual condition (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This null finding for the visual condition is explicitly stated and referenced to a figure.

claim: After correction for multiple comparisons, only intervals of 650, 750, and 850 ms showed a significant association between the behavioral and structural parameters.
source: After correction for multiple comparisons (pcft < 0.001 and pcluster < 0.001), only intervals of 650, 750, and 850 ms showed a significant association between the behavioral and structural parameters.
evidence: This finding is reported after statistical correction for multiple comparisons.

claim: Nine clusters (with 2232 vertices), twelve clusters (with 2827 vertices), and two clusters (with 374 vertices) showed significant correlations between auditory asynchronies and tanAFD for the 650, 750, and 850 ms intervals, respectively.
source: Indeed, nine (with 2232 vertices), twelve (with 2827 vertices), and two (with 374 vertices) clusters showed significant correlations between auditory asynchronies and tanAFD for the 650, 750, and 850 ms intervals, respectively.
evidence: These specific numbers of clusters and vertices are reported from the analysis.

claim: At a depth of 1.5 mm, the regions with a larger percent of significant vertices for the right hemisphere at 750 ms were the medial premotor (SMA and preSMA), auditory, and language motor areas.
source: At a depth of 1.5 mm, the regions with a larger percent of significant vertices for the right hemisphere at 750 ms were the medial premotor (supplementary motor area [SMA] and preSMA), auditory, and language motor areas (B).
evidence: This anatomical specificity is reported from the analysis and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The highest correlation in the canonical correlation analysis was found between the SCT data and the tanAFD, closely followed by totalAFD, and then parAFD.
source: Notably, all pairings of behavioral and AFD data rendered highly correlated canonical variates (Figure 6A). In line with the previous results, the highest correlation was found between the SCT data and the tanAFD, closely followed by totalAFD, and then parAFD (Figure 6A).
evidence: This ranking of correlations is reported from the canonical correlation analysis and shown in a figure.

claim: The asynchronies of the auditory modality for the 650–850 ms intervals are the parameters with a significant relation to the canonical variate.
source: Figure 6B depicts the correlations between each standardized SCT parameter and the corresponding canonical variate (U), where it is evident that the asynchronies of the auditory modality for the 650–850 ms intervals are the parameters with a significant relation to the canonical variate.
evidence: This finding from the canonical correlation analysis is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The FBA revealed significant negative correlations between the FDC in the CC and the absolute asynchronies to the auditory metronome for 650, 750, 850, and 950 ms intervals.
source: The FBA revealed significant negative correlations between the FDC in the CC and the absolute asynchronies to the auditory metronome for 650, 750, 850, and 950 ms intervals (Figure 7).
evidence: This finding from fixel-based analysis is reported and shown in Figure 7.

claim: Subjects exhibiting large phase accuracy with asynchronies close to zero showed large FDC values, and subjects with poor phase accuracy and large asynchronies had low FDC values.
source: Subjects exhibiting large phase accuracy with asynchronies close to zero also showed large FDC values, and subjects with poor phase accuracy and large asynchronies had low FDC values (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This relationship between behavioral and structural measures is reported and shown in a figure.

claim: The FDC fixel values of the posterior midbody of the CC showed a significant negative correlation with absolute auditory asynchronies for the 650 and 750 ms intervals.
source: Thus, the FDC fixel values of the posterior midbody of the CC (interconnecting motor and premotor cortices and M1) showed a significant negative correlation with absolute auditory asynchronies for the 650 and 750 ms intervals (Figure 7BC; family-wise error-corrected p-value <0.05).
evidence: This anatomically specific correlation is reported with statistical correction and shown in a figure.

claim: For the asynchronies at the intermediate interval of 850 ms, a negative correlation was observed with FDC fixel values located in the isthmus and the splenium.
source: For the asynchronies at the intermediate interval of 850 ms, a negative correlation was observed with FDC fixel values located in the isthmus and the splenium (Figure 7C; interconnecting primary motor, temporal, and visual cortices).
evidence: This anatomically specific correlation is reported and shown in a figure.

claim: The asynchronies of the 950 ms interval showed a significant negative correlation with fixels located in forceps minor and major.
source: Finally, the asynchronies of the 950 ms interval showed a significant negative correlation with fixels located in forceps minor and major (Figure 7A, D; interconnecting prefrontal and visual cortices, respectively).
evidence: This anatomically specific correlation is reported and shown in a figure.

claim: For the auditory condition, the tracts with significant FC fixels were the left arcuate fasciculus, CC M1, forceps major, superior longitudinal fasciculus 2, and right fornix.
source: Notably, for the auditory condition, the tracts with significant FC fixels were the left arcuate fasciculus (Figure 8A, E), CC M1 (Figure 8C, E), forceps major (Figure 8B, D), superior longitudinal fasciculus 2 (Figure 8F), and right fornix (see Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: These specific tracts are identified from the analysis and shown in figures.

claim: The tapping phase and period during the SCT showed precision and accuracy, as well as error corrections that were biased toward auditory rather than visual metronomes.
source: Our study supports five conclusions: First, the tapping phase and period during the SCT showed precision and accuracy, as well as error corrections that were biased toward auditory rather than visual metronomes, thereby confirming previous observations.
evidence: This is stated as one of the main conclusions of the study.

claim: The right audiomotor system exhibited individual differences in SWM and U-fiber density that were correlated with the degree of phase accuracy of the tapping synchronization across subjects.
source: Second, the right audiomotor system exhibited individual differences in SWM and U-fiber density. These differences were correlated with the degree of phase accuracy of the tapping synchronization across subjects.
evidence: This is stated as one of the main conclusions of the study.

claim: The correlations between U-fiber density and phase accuracy were selective for the synchronization epoch of the auditory condition and were specific to the 650 and 750 ms intervals.
source: Notably, the correlations were selective for the synchronization epoch of the auditory condition and were specific to the 650 and 750 ms intervals.
evidence: This specificity is stated as part of the main conclusions.

claim: There was a significant association between the rhythmic entrainment phase and the density and bundle diameter of the CC, forming an interval-selective map with an anterior–posterior trend.
source: Third, there was a significant association between the rhythmic entrainment phase and the density and bundle diameter of the CC, forming an interval-selective map with an anterior–posterior trend.
evidence: This is stated as one of the main conclusions of the study.

claim: The fiber bundle diameter of the arcuate fasciculus, CC, forceps major, and superior longitudinal fasciculus showed a significant correlation with the mean asynchronies across all tested tempos.
source: Fourth, the fiber bundle diameter of the arcuate fasciculus, CC, forceps major, and superior longitudinal fasciculus showed a significant correlation with the mean asynchronies across all tested tempos.
evidence: This is stated as one of the main conclusions of the study.

claim: No significant associations were found between SWM and DWM properties and temporal variability, constant error, or lag 1 autocorrelation under the visual and auditory conditions during the synchronization and continuation epochs of the SCT.
source: Finally, we found no significant associations between SWM and DWM properties and temporal variability, constant error, or lag 1 autocorrelation under the visual and auditory conditions during the synchronization and continuation epochs of the SCT.
evidence: This null finding is stated as one of the main conclusions.

claim: Performance tapping synchronized to an auditory metronome is more precise and accurate than synchronization to a flashing visual metronome with the same timing characteristics.
source: Many studies have shown that performance tapping synchronized to an auditory metronome is more precise and accurate than synchronization to a flashing visual metronome with the same timing characteristics (Chen et al., 2002; Hove et al., 2013; Merchant et al., 2008c; Patel et al., 2005; Repp and Penel, 2004; Zarco et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The auditory–visual asymmetry in synchronization can be cancelled out by visual moving metronomes.
source: This auditory–visual asymmetry can be cancelled out by visual moving metronomes (Hove et al., 2010; Pérez et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using moving visual stimuli.

claim: The auditory system has higher temporal resolution compared to the visual system since the first processing relays.
source: Since the first processing relays, the auditory system has higher temporal resolution compared to the visual system (Duysens et al., 1996; He et al., 1997; Sayegh et al., 2011) and plays a critical role in time perception and reproduction across many tasks, not only in tapping SCTs (Grondin et al., 2005; Merchant et al., 2008b; Merchant and de Lafuente, 2014c).
evidence: This claim about sensory system differences is supported by multiple citations.

claim: When audiovisual stimuli are used in an oddball paradigm, the perceived duration is dominated by the auditory modality.
source: For example, when audiovisual stimuli are used in an oddball paradigm, the perceived duration is dominated by the auditory modality (Chen and Yeh, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) disruption of the auditory cortex impaired time estimation for auditory and visual stimuli, while disruption in the visual cortex only produced timing impairments for visual stimuli.
source: In addition, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) disruption of the auditory cortex impaired time estimation for auditory and visual stimuli, while disruption in the visual cortex only produced timing impairments for visual stimuli (Kanai et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim about TMS effects is supported by a citation.

claim: The auditory cortex is engaged in multimodal temporal processing.
source: Consequently, a current hypothesis is that the auditory cortex is engaged in multimodal temporal processing, and the interaction between the auditory and motor systems in the frontal lobe allows not only time encoding but also time prediction (Merchant and Honing, 2014b; Merchant and Yarrow, 2016; Patel and Iversen, 2014; Schwartze et al., 2012).
evidence: This hypothesis is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The fiber bundle diameter of the left arcuate fasciculus showed a significant correlation with the mean asynchronies across all tested tempos.
source: Third, the fiber bundle diameter of the left arcuate fasciculus, a key tract connecting the parietotemporal auditory system with the frontal lobe, showed a significant correlation with the mean asynchronies across all tested tempos.
evidence: This specific finding about the arcuate fasciculus is stated in the discussion.

claim: The clustering of subjects as either good or bad synchronizers in a syllabic isochronous entrainment task correlates with both the difference in the activation magnitude in frontal areas and the changes in white matter pathways (i.e., left arcuate fasciculus) that connect the auditory system with the premotor cortical system.
source: Furthermore, the clear clustering of subjects as either good or bad synchronizers in a syllabic isochronous entrainment task correlates with both the difference in the activation magnitude in frontal areas and the changes in white matter pathways (i.e., left arcuate fasciculus) that connect the auditory system with the premotor cortical system (Assaneo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The lack of structural associations in the visual condition is probably due to the larger variability in rhythmic tapping for this modality.
source: The lack of structural associations in the visual condition is probably due to the larger variability in rhythmic tapping for this modality, making it difficult to infer statistical correlations between our metrics.
evidence: This is an interpretation offered by the authors to explain a null finding.

claim: The null anatomo-behavioral associations for the visual condition could be due to the slow sampling rate of visual periodic temporal attention, with a sampling interval that is longer than the tested durations.
source: As described above, the null anatomo-behavioral associations for the visual condition could also be due to the slow sampling rate of visual periodic temporal attention, with a sampling interval that is longer than our tested durations (Zalta et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an alternative explanation offered by the authors with a supporting citation.

claim: The associations between the measured SWM and DWM properties and the accuracy in the synchronization phase were negative.
source: The observed associations between the measured SWM and DWM properties and the accuracy in the synchronization phase were negative.
evidence: This describes the direction of the correlations found in the study.

claim: The white matter parameter values were greater in subjects with asynchronies close to zero and an accurate tapping phase with the metronome than in subjects with large gaps in time between the stimuli and taps.
source: This result indicates that the white matter parameter values were greater in subjects with asynchronies close to zero and an accurate tapping phase with the metronome than in subjects with large gaps in time between the stimuli and taps.
evidence: This interpretation of the negative correlations is stated in the discussion.

claim: Intersubject differences in rhythmic entrainment phase depend on micro- and macrostructural white matter properties, which could have a genetic and/or learned substrate.
source: These results support the theory that intersubject differences in rhythmic entrainment phase depend on micro- and macrostructural white matter properties, which could have a genetic and/or learned substrate.
evidence: This is an interpretation and theoretical claim made by the authors based on their findings.

claim: The existence of poor and superior synchronizers may depend on the FD of superficial U-fibers in the right audiomotor system, as well as on the density of deep tracts such as the CC and arcuate fasciculus.
source: From a genetics perspective, we could speculate that the existence of poor and superior synchronizers (Blecher et al., 2016) may depend on the FD of superficial U-fibers in the right audiomotor system, as well as on the density of deep tracts such as the CC and arcuate fasciculus.
evidence: This is a speculative claim made by the authors based on their findings.

claim: SWM and DWM bundles may develop larger density and myelination during intense musical practice, distinguishing the audiomotor tracts between musicians and non-musicians.
source: From a training perspective, these SWM and DWM bundles may develop larger density and myelination during intense musical practice, distinguishing the audiomotor tracts between musicians and non-musicians (Palomar-García et al., 2020; Vaquero et al., 2018; Zatorre et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about training effects, supported by citations.

claim: The interval specificity in the associations suggests that the preferred tempo for rhythmic entrainment has its origins in the structural properties of the U-fibers running superficially across the audiomotor circuit.
source: The interval specificity in these associations suggests that the preferred tempo for rhythmic entrainment has its origins in the structural properties of the U-fibers running superficially across the audiomotor circuit.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim made by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Cortico-cortical connectivity within the audiomotor system is especially designed to support the internal representation of an auditory beat at the preferred tempo, providing larger phase-locking abilities with the metronome for spontaneous motor tempos.
source: Consequently, we suggest that cortico-cortical connectivity within the audiomotor system is especially designed to support the internal representation of an auditory beat at the preferred tempo, providing larger phase-locking abilities with the metronome for spontaneous motor tempos (Balasubramaniam et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim made by the authors with a supporting citation.

claim: It is possible that no effects were found in the visual condition because the target interval of 950 ms was not slow enough for this modality.
source: Therefore, it is possible that we did not get effects in the visual condition because our target interval of 950 ms was not slow enough for this modality.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation offered by the authors for a null finding.

claim: Ultra-high-field (7T) functional imaging revealed that the medial premotor areas (SMA and pre-SMA) of the human brain possess neural circuits that are tuned to different durations, forming a topographical arrangement during a visual discrimination task.
source: Ultra-high-field (7T) functional imaging revealed that the medial premotor areas (SMA and pre-SMA) of the human brain possess neural circuits that are tuned to different durations, forming a topographical arrangement during a visual discrimination task.
evidence: This claim about chronomaps is supported by citations to imaging studies.

claim: Chronomaps show units with enhanced responses for the preferred interval and suppressed activity for the non-preferred duration, and define a topographical gradient with short preferred intervals in the anterior portion and long preferred intervals in the posterior portion of the medial premotor areas.
source: These chronomaps show units with enhanced responses for the preferred interval and suppressed activity for the non-preferred duration, and define a topographical gradient with short preferred intervals in the anterior portion and long preferred intervals in the posterior portion of the medial premotor areas (Protopapa et al., 2019; Schwartze et al., 2012).
evidence: This description of chronomaps is supported by citations.

claim: Chronomaps represent relative rather than absolute time, and they present some flexibility in the location of the preferred interval depending on the task context.
source: Notably, chronomaps also showed an anterior–posterior gradient, but they represent relative rather than absolute time, and they presented some flexibility in the location of the preferred interval depending on the task context (Bueti et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim about the nature of chronomaps is supported by a citation.

claim: A recent imaging study described the existence of large chronomaps covering the cortical mantle from the dorsal and ventral premotor areas to the occipital pole.
source: In addition, a recent imaging study described the existence of large chronomaps covering the cortical mantle from the dorsal and ventral premotor areas to the occipital pole (Harvey et al., 2020; Hendrikx et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent imaging studies.

claim: The interval-selective map found in this study is defined by the correlation between asynchronies and FDA, with no topographic model of the distribution of preferred intervals as shown in fMRI studies.
source: Nevertheless, our interval-selective map is defined by the correlation between asynchronies and FDA, with no topographic model of the distribution of preferred intervals as shown in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies.
evidence: This distinguishes the current findings from previous fMRI studies.

claim: The map for duration selectivity starts anteriorly in the CC, which is linked to the premotor system, and ends in the CC of the visual areas of the occipital lobe.
source: These findings suggest that the map for duration selectivity starts anteriorly in the CC, which is linked to the premotor system, and ends in the CC of the visual areas of the occipital lobe.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the topographic findings made by the authors.

claim: The anterior selectivity for the 650 and 750 ms ISI supports the notion that the motor system functions at 1.7 Hz during beat perception and entrainment and strongly influences the auditory system but not the visual system at this tempo.
source: The anterior selectivity for the 650 and 750 ms ISI supports the notion that the motor system functions at 1.7 Hz during beat perception and entrainment and strongly influences the auditory system but not the visual system at this tempo (Zalta et al., 2020).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by a citation to Zalta et al., 2020.

claim: Timing maps define a cortical processing framework for efficient timing integration that has both functional and anatomical bases, especially for the auditory modality.
source: Consequently, timing maps define a cortical processing framework for efficient timing integration that has both functional and anatomical bases, especially for the auditory modality (Merchant and de Lafuente, 2024a).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim made by the authors with a supporting citation.

claim: Blecher et al., 2016 found a positive association between the fractional anisotropy of the left arcuate fasciculus and CC and performance in an auditory-cued finger-tapping task.
source: For instance, Blecher et al., 2016 found a positive association between the fractional anisotropy of the left arcuate fasciculus and CC and performance in an auditory-cued finger-tapping task.
evidence: This claim about a previous study is supported by a citation.

claim: The SWM immediately below the cortex accounts for 60% of the total white matter volume and is pivotal in maintaining cortico-cortical connectivity.
source: The SWM immediately below the cortex has received has been less studied than DWM fasciculi, even though it accounts for 60% of the total white matter volume and is pivotal in maintaining cortico-cortical connectivity (Schüz and Braitenberg, 2002; Schmahmann et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim about SWM is supported by citations.

claim: Recent studies have implicated SWM abnormalities in epilepsy, autism spectrum disorder, Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, and stroke.
source: Nonetheless, recent studies have implicated SWM abnormalities in epilepsy (Liu et al., 2016), autism spectrum disorder (Hong et al., 2019), Alzheimer's disease (Phillips et al., 2016), schizophrenia (Nazeri et al., 2013), and stroke (Stockert et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim about clinical relevance is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The SWM contains short-range association fibers that connect adjacent gyri (U-fibers) and the initial or final portions of long-range connections that traverse the DWM.
source: The SWM contains short-range association fibers that connect adjacent gyri (U-fibers) and the initial or final portions of long-range connections that traverse the DWM (Schüz and Braitenberg, 2002; Guevara et al., 2020; Kirilina et al., 2020; Yoshino et al., 2020).
evidence: This anatomical description is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The SWM is difficult to study because of its complicated geometry and abundance of fiber crossings.
source: The SWM is difficult to study because of its complicated geometry and abundance of fiber crossings (Guevara et al., 2020).
evidence: This methodological challenge is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Better performance in a bimanual coordination task was associated with higher FBA values in the CC.
source: For example, better performance in a bimanual coordination task was associated with higher FBA values in the CC (Zivari Adab et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim about a previous study is supported by a citation.

claim: Thirty-two healthy human subjects without musical training volunteered to participate in the study.
source: Thirty-two healthy human subjects (age = 25.37 ± 3.21 years; 19 females) without musical training volunteered to participate and gave informed consent, which complied with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by our Institutional Review Board.
evidence: This describes the participant sample used in the study.

claim: All participants were right-handed and native Spanish speakers.
source: All participants were right-handed and native Spanish speakers.
evidence: This describes characteristics of the participant sample.

claim: Participants did not have MRI contraindications or neurological, psychiatric, or cognitive conditions.
source: They did not have MRI contraindications or neurological, psychiatric, or cognitive conditions.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for the study.

claim: The isochronous target intervals were 550, 650, 750, 850, and 950 ms.
source: The isochronous target intervals were 550, 650, 750, 850, and 950 ms, which were pseudorandomly presented within a block.
evidence: This describes the experimental design parameters.

claim: Each subject performed 10 correct trials for each target interval.
source: Each subject performed 10 correct trials for each target interval.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The MRIs were collected in the first session, and in a second visit, the auditory and visual tasks were performed randomly across subjects outside of the MRI scanner.
source: The MRIs were collected in the first session. In a second visit, the auditory and visual tasks were performed randomly across subjects outside of the MRI scanner.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Images were acquired using a 3T Philips Achieva TX scanner with a 32-channel head coil.
source: Images were acquired using a 3T Philips Achieva TX scanner with a 32-channel head coil.
evidence: This describes the imaging equipment used.

claim: AFD is proportional to the total intra-axonal volume, thus reflecting the density of a population of fibers within a voxel.
source: FD is derived from the integral of the fiber orientation distribution (FOD) lobes and is proportional to the total intra-axonal volume, thus reflecting the density of a population of fibers within a voxel (Rojas-Vite et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the FD metric with a supporting citation.

claim: FC is a macroscopic metric of the fiber bundle diameter.
source: FC is a macroscopic metric of the fiber bundle diameter and, finally, FDC is a combination of FD and FC (see Methods).
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the FC metric.

claim: The average depth of the U-fiber system is approximately 1.5 mm.
source: According to Schüz and Braitenberg, 2002, the average depth of the U-fiber system is approximately 1.5 mm.
evidence: This anatomical fact is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Data for one subject was discarded for SWM analysis due to suboptimal registration between DWI metric maps and white matter surface.
source: Data for one subject was discarded for SWM analysis (Figures 3—5) due to suboptimal registration between DWI metric maps and white matter surface.
evidence: This describes a data exclusion in the analysis.

claim: parAFD is related to association, commissural, and projection fibers that eventually enter or exit DWM bundles.
source: Throughout this work, we assume that parAFD is related to association, commissural, and projection fibers that eventually enter or exit DWM bundles, while tanAFD is informative of short-range cortico-cortical connections through U-fibers (Schüz and Braitenberg, 2002).
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the parAFD metric with a supporting citation.

claim: tanAFD is informative of short-range cortico-cortical connections through U-fibers.
source: Throughout this work, we assume that parAFD is related to association, commissural, and projection fibers that eventually enter or exit DWM bundles, while tanAFD is informative of short-range cortico-cortical connections through U-fibers (Schüz and Braitenberg, 2002).
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the tanAFD metric with a supporting citation.
